title: REG U1·W1 — Ethics, Professional Responsibilities & Federal Tax Procedures (CPA Core · from CMA m12)
lessonHtml:
Cold open — the tax preparer's own rulebook

REG is the CPA section where you become the tax adviser, and before any number reaches a return there is a body of rules governing how a preparer must behave. When Jordan Reed's construction company MBG files its returns, the CPA who signs them is bound by Treasury Circular 230, the Internal Revenue Code's preparer-penalty regime, and the AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services. CMA month 12 covered ethics from the management accountant's seat; REG adds the tax practitioner's distinct duties and the real penalties for breaching them.

Circular 230 — practice before the IRS

Circular 230 is issued by the Treasury Department and governs who may practice before the IRS and how. Those with unlimited practice rights are attorneys, CPAs, and enrolled agents (EAs); enrolled actuaries and enrolled retirement plan agents have limited rights. A practitioner's core duties include exercising due diligence as to the accuracy of returns and representations; promptly submitting records the IRS lawfully requests; not charging an unconscionable fee and not charging a contingent fee except in narrow situations (such as an examination or a claim for refund); avoiding conflicts of interest unless each affected client gives informed written consent; and not unreasonably delaying a matter before the IRS. A practitioner must also advise a client of any noncompliance, error, or omission and its consequences — but Circular 230 does not require the practitioner to notify the IRS of the client's error.

Circular 230 sanctions

The Office of Professional Responsibility (OPR) enforces Circular 230. For incompetence or disreputable conduct, willful violations, or recklessly giving false opinions, the Treasury may censure (a public reprimand), suspend, or disbar a practitioner from practice before the IRS, and may impose a monetary penalty up to the gross income derived from the offending conduct. Disbarment requires willful, reckless, or grossly incompetent conduct — not a mere good-faith mistake.

Preparer penalties under the Code

The Internal Revenue Code imposes its own penalties on paid preparers. §6694 targets understatements from unreasonable positions: a position lacking substantial authority (or, if disclosed, lacking a reasonable basis; for a tax shelter or reportable transaction the bar rises to more likely than not) triggers a penalty of the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the income the preparer derived from the return. If the understatement is willful or reckless, the penalty rises to the greater of $5,000 or 75% of that income. §6695 imposes smaller fixed penalties for procedural failures — failing to sign the return, failing to furnish the taxpayer a copy, failing to keep records, failing to provide a preparer tax identification number (PTIN), or negotiating a client's refund check. §6713 and §7216 penalize the unauthorized disclosure or use of taxpayer information, with §7216 carrying criminal exposure.

The reporting-standards ladder

Several confidence thresholds recur, and the exam tests their order. From lowest to highest: frivolous (not arguable); reasonable basis (roughly a 20%-or-greater chance of success — the minimum for a disclosed position); substantial authority (roughly 40%, the standard for an undisclosed position); more likely than not (greater than 50%, required for tax shelters and to avoid certain penalties); and, highest in practice, a should/will opinion. Adequate disclosure of a position is made on Form 8275 (or 8275-R for a position contrary to a regulation), which can reduce both preparer and taxpayer penalties when the position has a reasonable basis.

AICPA Statements on Standards for Tax Services

The SSTS are enforceable standards for AICPA members in tax practice. Their core rules: a member should not recommend a position unless it meets the applicable reporting standard, and should advise the client of potential penalties; a member may rely in good faith on client-provided information but should make reasonable inquiries when information appears incorrect, incomplete, or inconsistent; a member may use the taxpayer's estimates if reasonable under the circumstances and not presented as exact; on learning of an error in a previously filed return, the member should advise the client to correct it but may not notify the IRS without the client's consent (except where the law requires it); and advice should reflect professional competence and serve the client's needs. The SSTS parallel Circular 230 but are AICPA-enforced and apply specifically to members.

Taxpayer penalties

Separate from the preparer, the taxpayer faces penalties. The accuracy-related penalty (§6662) is 20% of the underpayment attributable to negligence, disregard of rules, or a substantial understatement (for an individual, generally more than the greater of 10% of the correct tax or $5,000). The civil fraud penalty (§6663) is 75% of the portion of the underpayment due to fraud. Failure to file (§6651) runs at 5% per month (up to 25%), while failure to pay runs at 0.5% per month; in a month when both apply, the failure-to-file penalty is reduced by the failure-to-pay amount. A reasonable-cause defense, shown by good-faith effort, can abate many of these — but never fraud.

Statutes of limitations and the audit path

The IRS generally must assess additional tax within three years of the later of the due date or the filing date. That extends to six years if the taxpayer omits more than 25% of gross income, and is unlimited for a false or fraudulent return or a failure to file. A taxpayer's refund claim must be filed within the later of three years from filing or two years from payment. A disputed examination goes first to IRS Appeals, an independent function that weighs the hazards of litigation; unresolved cases proceed to the U.S. Tax Court (no prepayment of the tax required), or to a U.S. District Court or the Court of Federal Claims after the taxpayer pays the tax and sues for a refund. These procedures, the penalty regime, and the practitioner standards together define the compliance environment in which every later REG topic is applied.

Bringing it to the construction client

For MBG these rules are concrete. If the CPA takes an aggressive position on the deductibility of a large equipment expenditure, the position needs substantial authority to go undisclosed, or a reasonable basis plus a Form 8275 disclosure, or the preparer risks the §6694 penalty. If Jordan Reed supplies an estimate of materials consumed on an in-progress job, the SSTS permit a reasonable estimate that is not held out as precise. And if the prior-year return overstated a deduction, the CPA must advise correction but cannot go behind the client to the IRS. The professional-responsibility layer is, in short, the frame around the tax computations the rest of REG teaches — get the duty and the standard right before you get the number right.

CMA bridge

CMA month 12 taught the IMA ethics standards for the internal management accountant; REG covers the tax practitioner's parallel but distinct duties under Circular 230 and the SSTS, plus the statutory penalties the IMA framework never reaches. Both demand integrity and a refusal to misrepresent — REG adds the federal enforcement teeth.

Practice and recap

  1. Know who has unlimited practice rights (attorneys, CPAs, EAs) and the core Circular 230 duties.
  2. Apply the §6694 preparer penalty (greater of $1,000/50%; willful or reckless, $5,000/75%).
  3. Order the standards: reasonable basis (disclosed) < substantial authority (undisclosed) < more likely than not (shelters).
  4. Distinguish the §6662 20% accuracy penalty from the §6663 75% fraud penalty, and know the 3/6/unlimited-year assessment statutes.

Recap: Circular 230 and the SSTS govern how a preparer must act; an undisclosed position needs substantial authority while a disclosed one needs reasonable basis (Form 8275); the §6694 preparer penalty is the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the fee; taxpayers face a 20% accuracy or 75% fraud penalty; and assessment is generally 3 years, 6 if more than 25% of gross income is omitted, and unlimited for fraud.

flashcards.front: Who has UNLIMITED practice rights before the IRS?
flashcards.back: Attorneys, CPAs, and enrolled agents (EAs). Enrolled actuaries/retirement plan agents have limited rights.
Greater of $1,000 or 50% of the preparer's income from the return; willful/reckless raises it to the greater of $5,000 or 75%.

flashcards.front: Standard for an UNDISCLOSED return position
flashcards.back: Substantial authority (~40%). A disclosed position needs only a reasonable basis (~20%); shelters need more likely than not.

flashcards.front: Where is a position disclosed to reduce penalties?
flashcards.back: Form 8275 (Form 8275-R if contrary to a regulation).
20% of the underpayment (negligence, disregard of rules, or substantial understatement).
75% of the underpayment attributable to fraud.
3 years generally; 6 years if more than 25% of gross income is omitted; unlimited for a fraudulent return or no return.

flashcards.front: SSTS rule on a discovered error in a filed return
flashcards.back: Advise the client to correct it; do NOT notify the IRS without the client's consent.

questions.q: Who has UNLIMITED rights to practice before the IRS?
questions.explain: Attorneys, CPAs, and enrolled agents have unlimited practice rights; enrolled actuaries and retirement plan agents have limited rights.

questions.q: The §6694 penalty for a preparer's unreasonable position (not willful) is:
choices: The greater of $1,000 or 50% of the preparer's income from the return
questions.explain: §6694 is the greater of $1,000 or 50% of the preparer's income; willful or reckless conduct raises it to the greater of $5,000 or 75%.

questions.q: An UNDISCLOSED return position generally must meet which standard?
questions.explain: Undisclosed positions need substantial authority (~40%); a disclosed position needs only reasonable basis (~20%).

questions.q: A position is adequately DISCLOSED to reduce penalties on:
questions.explain: Form 8275 (or 8275-R for a position contrary to a regulation) makes the disclosure.
§6662 imposes a 20% penalty for negligence or a substantial understatement; §6663 fraud is 75%.

questions.q: The assessment statute of limitations extends to SIX years when the taxpayer:
choices: Omits more than 25% of gross income
questions.explain: Omitting more than 25% of gross income extends the statute to six years; fraud or no return is unlimited.

questions.q: Under the SSTS, a CPA who discovers an error in a client's previously filed return should:
choices: Advise the client to correct it; do not notify the IRS without consent
Resign and report to the SEC
questions.explain: The member advises the client to correct the error but may not notify the IRS without the client's consent.
